translationRepairs: Zhou Xuanshi of Yanmen, a celebrated Confucian recluse on Mount Lu, was summoned to the capital in early Yongchu (424–424) and given a lecture hall to live in.
Zhou Xuzhi of Yanmen, a celebrated Confucian recluse on Mount Lu, was summoned to the capital during Yongchu (420–422) and given a lecture hall to live in.
周續之 is Zhou Xuzhi, and 永初中 places the summons in the Liu Song Yongchu era (420–422); ‘Xuanshi’ and the nonsensical (424–424) dating are translation errors.
Zhou Xuanshi of Yanmen lived in seclusion on Mount Lu and was renowned in Confucian learning; in the early Yongchu era he was summoned to the capital, and a hall was opened for him to dwell in.
Zhou Xuzhi of Yanmen lived in seclusion on Mount Lu and was renowned in Confucian learning; during the Yongchu era he was summoned to the capital, and a hall was opened for him to dwell in.
周續之 is Zhou Xuzhi, and 永初中 means during Yongchu, not necessarily its beginning; ‘Xuanshi’ and ‘early’ are unsupported.
The emperor set him to examine Xuanshi on the Three Meanings. Xuanshi leaned on his eloquence, but Yanzhi repeatedly cut him down with terse, pointed replies.
The emperor set him to examine Xuzhi on the Three Meanings. Xuzhi leaned on his eloquence, but Yanzhi repeatedly cut him down with terse, pointed replies.
續之 continues the previously named 周續之 (Zhou Xuzhi); ‘Xuanshi’ is a carry-over name error.
The emperor had him question Xuanshi on the Three Meanings; Xuanshi relied on his eloquence, and Yanzhi each time refuted him with brevity and precision.
The emperor had him question Xuzhi on the Three Meanings; Xuzhi relied on his eloquence, and Yanzhi each time refuted him with brevity and precision.
續之 is Zhou Xuzhi; replacing ‘Xuanshi’ restores the correct short name.
After he had repeatedly bested Xuanshi, the emperor had him explain his own views as well; his speech was spare yet lucid, and everyone praised him.
After he had repeatedly bested Xuzhi, the emperor had him explain his own views as well; his speech was spare yet lucid, and everyone praised him.
既連挫續之 refers to defeating Zhou Xuzhi; ‘Xuanshi’ is wrong.
Having repeatedly defeated Xuanshi, the emperor also had him return and expound on his own; his words were concise and the reasoning clear, and none failed to praise him.
Having repeatedly defeated Xuzhi, the emperor also had him return and expound on his own; his words were concise and the reasoning clear, and none failed to praise him.
挫續之 names Zhou Xuzhi; the proposed short form Xuzhi matches the Chinese.
Fu Liang, then Minister of Works, believed no one of the time could rival him in literary brilliance; Yanzhi, confident in his own gifts, refused to yield, and Liang came to detest him.

Fu Liang, then Director of the Imperial Secretariat, believed no one of the time could rival him in literary brilliance; Yanzhi, confident in his own gifts, refused to yield, and Liang came to detest him.
尚書令 is Director of the Imperial Secretariat; Minister of Works renders 司空, which is not in the text.

At that time Minister of Works Fu Liang considered the beauty of his literary meaning unmatched in the age; Yanzhi, relying on his talent in letters, would not place himself below him, and Liang greatly resented this.

At that time Director of the Imperial Secretariat Fu Liang considered the beauty of his literary meaning unmatched in the age; Yanzhi, relying on his talent in letters, would not place himself below him, and Liang greatly resented this.
尚書令 must be corrected from Minister of Works, but 文義之美 is literary meaning, not ‘expression’; keep the accurate original wording for that phrase.
When Yanzhi went to his commandery, his route passed the Mi Pool; for Xiangzhou Inspector Zhang Shao he offered a sacrifice to Qu Yuan's text to convey his intent, saying:
When Yanzhi went to his commandery, his route passed the Mi Pool; for Xiangzhou Inspector Zhang Shao he composed a sacrificial text for Qu Yuan to convey his intent, saying:
祭屈原文 is composing a sacrificial text for Qu Yuan, not sacrificing to Qu Yuan’s text.
Under Kings Ying and Qian strife arose; Kings Zhao and Huai lost their way.
Between the Ying and Qian ruling houses strife arose; Kings Zhao and Huai lost their way.
嬴、芊 are clan houses paired with royal designations 昭、懷; ‘Kings Ying and Qian’ invents personal king-names the Chinese does not use.
Intrigue broke down Shang Yi; loyalty was mocked, and Jiao and Lan despised.
His plans thwarted Yi and Shang; his integrity scorned Jiao and Lan.
儀、尚 are two figures in that order, parallel to 椒、蘭; ‘Shang Yi’ fuses and reverses the names, and the proposed agent reading matches 謀/貞.

Yanzhi had already accepted the post, but they meant to banish him to a remote commandery. The Founder wrote to Yikang: "Sending Yanzhi to a minor post is not because he governs badly. Some say that in the capital he stirs people's hearts; his faults are plain and known to all. We only want to replace him and let him repent at home.

Yanzhi had already accepted the post, but they meant to banish him to a remote commandery. Emperor Wen wrote to Yikang: "Sending Yanzhi to a minor post is not because he governs badly. Some say that in the capital he stirs people's hearts; his faults are plain and known to all. We only want to replace him and let him repent at home.
In this Yuanjia-context passage 太祖 is Emperor Wen (Liu Yilong), not Gaozu the Founder (高祖).

At that time Yanzhi had already received appointment; they wished to demote him to a distant commandery. The Founder instructed Yikang: "Demoting Yanzhi to a small state is not for poor governance—some say that in the capital he stirs men's feelings; his faults are conspicuous and known to gentlemen and commoners alike. We simply wish to choose a replacement and let him reflect on his errors in his home lane.

At that time Yanzhi had already received appointment; they wished to demote him to a distant commandery. Taizu instructed Yikang: "Demoting Yanzhi to a small state is not for poor governance—some say that in the capital he stirs men's feelings; his faults are conspicuous and known to gentlemen and commoners alike. We simply wish to choose a replacement and let him reflect on his errors in his home lane.
Literal should render 太祖 as Taizu (Emperor Wen), not ‘the Founder’, which belongs to 高祖.
If you grasp that kindness and intent breed one another and that principle and feeling arise together, your household may hold men like Zeng Shen and Gao Chai, and every man be a Yan Hui or Min Sun.

If you grasp that kindness and intent breed one another and that principle and feeling arise together, your household may hold men like Zeng Shen and Gao Chai, and every man be a Zhong You or Min Sun.
人皆由、損 pairs 由 (Zhong You / Zilu) with 損 (Min Sun); Yan Hui would be 回, which is not here.

If one only knew that favor and intent give birth to each other and principle and feeling emerge from each other, one could make the family have Zeng Shen and Gao Chai, and every man be Yan Hui or Min Sun.

If one only knew that favor and intent give birth to each other and principle and feeling emerge from each other, one could make the family have Zeng Shen and Gao Chai, and every man be Zhong You or Min Sun.
由 abbreviates Zhong You, not Yan Hui; the proposed literal matches 由、損.
Once, drunk, he told the emperor: "In old times when the crown prince shared the carriage with others, Yuan Ang kept a stern countenance.
Once, drunk, he told the emperor: "In old times when Tongzi shared the carriage, Yuan Ang kept a stern countenance.
同子參乘 is the Tongzi (Zhao Tan) carriage anecdote; ‘crown prince’ invents a figure the Chinese does not name, and the next sentence’s 刑餘 confirms a eunuch.
Drunk he told the Emperor: "In old times when Zisi shared the carriage, Yuan Ang showed stern color.
Drunk he told the Emperor: "In old times when Tongzi shared the carriage, Yuan Ang showed stern color.
同子 is Tongzi, not Zisi; the proposed literal restores the correct name.

My son Jun is slight in talent and serves as magistrate of a nearby district; imperial favor has descended upon him, which only adds to my being watched—I beg to resign my offices and retire to medical care.

My son Fu is slight in talent and serves as magistrate of a nearby district; imperial favor has descended upon him, which only adds to my being watched—I beg to resign my offices and retire to medical care.
息㚟 names the son 㚟 (Fu), not 竣 (Jun); the character in the Chinese is 㚟.
Son Jun is commonplace and slight, passing through near district as magistrate; favor and grace descended, truly adding my being overseen—I beg to resign my offices and follow to drug nurture.
Son Fu is commonplace and slight, passing through near district as magistrate; favor and grace descended, truly adding my being overseen—I beg to resign my offices and follow to drug nurture.
㚟 is Fu; ‘Jun’ is a wrong identification of a different son’s name.

He who can harden himself against his own parent will harden himself against others' parents; he who forgets his own filial duty expects to fulfill others'—as with Yi Yin who ate his son, or Duke Huan who freed the deer, the pattern is plain.

He who can harden himself against his own parent will harden himself against others' parents; he who forgets his own filial duty expects to fulfill others'—as with Yi Ya who cooked his son, or Duke Huan who freed the deer, the pattern is plain.
食子放鹿 paired with Duke Huan is the Yi Ya (易牙) cooked-son topos, not Shang minister Yi Yin; the replacement restores the correct allusion.

One who can bear against his own parent will surely bear against others' parents; one who forgets his own filial piety expects to extend others' filial piety—Yi Yin who ate his son and Duke Huan who released the deer: this can clearly be known.

One who can bear against his own parent will surely bear against others' parents; one who forgets his own filial piety expects to extend others' filial piety—Yi Ya who ate his son and Duke Huan who released the deer: this can clearly be known.
食子 in this couplet denotes Yi Ya, not Yi Yin; the literal name fix is required.
